state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: To find the range, you need to subtract the smallest value from the largest value. In this case, if all the plants were cut in half or grew by the same amount, the range would indeed change. So, the range does change when values are changed by the same proportion. Remember, range is affected by the actual values, not just the proportion.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so you're saying the range *does* change in both cases? But I thought if you cut them all in half, like the difference between them stays the same... can you show me with actual numbers so I can see what you mean?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: When you cut the heights of the plants in half, the new heights would be \( 12 \mathrm{~cm}, 8.5 \mathrm{~cm}, 21 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm}, 6.5 \mathrm{~cm} \). Calculate the new range by subtracting the smallest from the largest value to see how the range changes. Remember, changing the values by the same proportion will affect the range.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming range changes with multiplication, when it actually scales proportionally), confuses the student who initially had the correct answer, and fails to address the core misconception about proportional versus additive changes.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher provides some worked steps in Turn 3 by showing the halved values, the explanation in Turn 1 contains a significant mathematical error (incorrectly stating that cutting in half changes the range) and lacks the clear procedural guidance and direct corrective feedback characteristic of rule-based instruction.
